traveler: St. Anthony of Padua (Fernando Martins de Bulhões)
title: The Tongue That Would Not Rot: Lisbon to Padua by way of a Shipwreck
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lisbon, the house by the cathedral: a son of the Bulhões
stops.date_confidence: the year and the city are attested; the day of 15 August is traditional and is not carried by any contemporary document
stops.campa: A son is born to a family of the city's minor nobility, in a house within sight of the Sé, the cathedral raised over the mosque of a city taken from Islam only forty years before. They name him Fernando Martins de Bulhões. His father is remembered as Vicente Martins, his mother as Teresa Pais Taveira, and the historian who repeats the names says plainly that the parentage is uncertain. Lisbon is a port, and Morocco is a week's sailing south. The Church of Santo António now stands on the ground where the house stood.
suggested_refs: The Igreja de Santo António de Lisboa, built over the traditional site of the birth-house
sources: New Advent, Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'St. Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: São Vicente de Fora, the Augustinian habit at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as c. 1210; no month or day in any source
stops.campa: At about fifteen he enters the Canons Regular of the Holy Cross at the abbey of São Vicente de Fora, outside the walls, and takes on the choir, the rule, and the Latin. The house is close enough to his family's that his friends keep coming to the gate. A canon regular is not a wanderer: he is a man attached to a church for life, singing the offices in the same stall until he dies in it. Fernando is professed in that life at fifteen and leaves it at twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The Mosteiro de São Vicente de Fora, Lisbon, in its pre-Habsburg fabric

stops.name: Coimbra, Santa Cruz: the transfer inland
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1212 by both encyclopedias; no month
stops.campa: He asks to be moved to the Augustinian motherhouse at Coimbra, the reason given in every account being that the visits of friends and family in Lisbon will not let him study. Santa Cruz holds the best library in Portugal, and the first two kings of Portugal are buried in it. In this room he assembles, page by page, the command of scripture that will later silence a papal court. He reads for eight years. No document from any of those years mentions him by name.
stops.quote: Just as the root feeds the tree, so humility feeds the soul. The spirit of humility is sweeter than honey, and whoever is fed by this sweetness produces fruit.
stops.quote_source: Sermon for the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost, Sermones Dominicales et Festivi, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The library and scriptorium of the Mosteiro de Santa Cruz, Coimbra

stops.name: Coimbra, the bodies of the five come back from Morocco
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1220; the month of the relics' arrival is not given
stops.campa: Five Franciscans who went to Morocco to preach are killed there, and their bodies are carried back to Coimbra and laid in the church of the canons. Fernando, twenty-five, goes to look at them. What the friars offer is precisely what his own order does not: a road out, a foreign language, and an ending. He asks leave to go. The canons resist, then let him go, and he tells the brothers who are losing him that he will pray for them when he is a saint in Morocco.
suggested_refs: The five Franciscan protomartyrs of Morocco, killed at Marrakesh in January 1220

stops.name: Santo António dos Olivais, the change of habit and of name
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1220; no month or day, and the sequence with the martyrs' arrival is given only as an order of events
stops.campa: On a hillside outside Coimbra stands a hermitage of the small new order, its chapel dedicated to Anthony the Great, the Egyptian who went into the desert nine centuries earlier and made solitude a profession. Fernando puts off the white of the canons and puts on the grey, and takes the hermit's name for his own. From here forward the record calls him Anthony. Two saints will carry the name into Spanish American villages, and the villages will not always keep them apart: the one with the pig and the tau, the one with the lily and the book.
suggested_refs: The Igreja de Santo António dos Olivais, Coimbra, on the site of the Franciscan hermitage
sources: OpenStreetMap, Igreja de Santo António dos Olivais

stops.name: Morocco, the winter of the illness
stops.date_confidence: the Italian tradition dates the sailing to autumn 1220; English Wikipedia dates it 1221, and the port of landing is named by no reachable source
stops.campa: He sails for Morocco to preach to the Almohad court and to be killed for it, the whole design of his new life fitting into one sentence. He is on African ground for a season and preaches to no one. Marrakesh, where the five died, he never reaches. A sickness takes him almost at once and does not let go through the winter; the sources do not agree on what it was. In the spring they carry him down to the water and put him aboard a ship for Portugal, a friar of a few months who has failed at the only thing he changed orders to do.
suggested_refs: The Almohad court at Marrakesh, intended destination of the mission

stops.name: The coast between Tusa and Caronia, the ship driven ashore
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia places the wreck on the Sicilian coast in late 1220; no day is recorded
stops.campa: The ship is bound for Portugal and a storm takes it in the open sea for days. It comes apart at last on the northern shore of Sicily, between Tusa and Caronia, a coast of shingle and low cliffs that the passengers had no reason to be looking at. Anthony comes out of the water sick and penniless, in the last weeks of 1220, about as far from both Lisbon and Marrakesh as the Mediterranean can put a man. Nobody records how many others came ashore with him.
suggested_refs: The Tyrrhenian coast of the Nebrodi between Tusa and Caronia

stops.name: Messina, taken in by the friars
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia gives spring 1221 for the arrival at Messina
stops.campa: The Franciscans of Messina take in the shipwrecked stranger and nurse him back through the spring. He says nothing about Coimbra, nothing about eight years of theology, nothing about the library. From these brothers he hears that the whole order is to gather at Assisi at Pentecost, every friar who can walk there, and he decides that he can walk there. Assisi is the whole length of Italy away, and he is still weak; the walk takes him the rest of the spring.
suggested_refs: The early Franciscan house at Messina, first Franciscan foundation in Sicily

stops.name: The Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats
stops.date_confidence: attested; the number of friars present is given variously as three thousand and five thousand
stops.campa: Thousands of friars camp in the fields around the little chapel, sleeping under mats of woven reed, and Francis of Assisi presides over them sitting on the ground. Assignments are read out and the provinces divided. Anthony has no province and no post; he is a Portuguese nobody who came off a wreck, and when the chapter breaks up he has to ask a minister to take him anywhere at all. Brother Gratian of Romagna agrees to have him. Nobody in the field records his name.
suggested_refs: The Porziuncola, Santa Maria degli Angeli, and the Pentecost general chapter of 1221
sources: saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats'

stops.name: Montepaolo, the hermitage above Dovadola
stops.date_confidence: attested as following immediately on the 1221 chapter; no precise month
stops.campa: Six friars live on a wooded ridge above the Montone valley, and Anthony is sent to be their priest. He says their Mass and otherwise asks for the kitchen: he washes the pots, sweeps, and by one account keeps a cave below the house for prayer. For more than a year the brothers he lives with have no idea that the quiet Portuguese can read Augustine in Latin at speed. He does not tell them. The cave below the house is still shown to pilgrims at Dovadola.
stops.quote: He said not a word of his studies, nor of the services he had performed; his only desire was to follow Jesus Christ and Him crucified.
stops.quote_source: Anthony's earliest, anonymous biographer, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Eremo di Montepaolo at Dovadola, with the cave cell shown to pilgrims

stops.name: Forlì, the sermon nobody had prepared
stops.date_confidence: attested as 1222; the occasion is an ordination, the month unrecorded
stops.campa: Franciscans and Dominicans come into Forlì for an ordination, and at the meal afterwards it emerges that no one has readied a sermon: each order assumed the other would speak. The superior turns to the dishwasher from Montepaolo and tells him to say whatever the Holy Spirit puts in his mouth. Anthony stands up and preaches, without notes, in ordered Latin, moving through scripture as a man moves through his own house. He is taken off kitchen duty and sent out to preach through Romagna.
stops.quote: The saints are like the stars, who, in His providence, Christ hides under a seal, lest they appear whenever they wish. Instead, they are always ready to disembark from the quiet of contemplation into the works of mercy at the time decided upon by God, whenever their heart should hear the word of command.
stops.quote_source: Sermon for the Fifth Sunday after Easter, Sermones Dominicales et Festivi, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Santa Croce at Forlì, site of the 1222 ordination

stops.name: Rimini, the shore and the fish
stops.date_confidence: legend; no year, no contemporary attestation, and the earliest written carrier could not be identified
stops.campa: Sent to preach in a town thick with heretics, he is met with turned backs and shut doors. So he walks down to where the river runs into the Adriatic and preaches to the water instead. The fish come up, the story says, and hold themselves in ranks with their heads above the surface, the small ones in front, the large behind, until he finishes and blesses them, and the townspeople who came to laugh stay to listen. Of the words he used to the fish not one syllable is recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Rimini fish sermon in later Franciscan legendary, and Mahler's setting in Des Knaben Wunderhorn

stops.name: Rimini, the mule that would not eat
stops.date_confidence: legend; undated, and other tellings move the whole scene to Toulouse or Bourges
stops.campa: A man named in the tellings as Bononillo, or Bonovillo, will not accept that Christ is present in the Eucharist and proposes a test: starve a mule three days, then set fodder before it beside the Host, and let the animal decide. The town comes out to watch. The mule is brought, the fodder is laid down, Anthony lifts the monstrance, and the animal turns from the food and goes down on its knees. A small temple later marks the spot. Two other cities claim the same event on their own ground.
suggested_refs: The tempietto at Rimini marking the traditional site of the Eucharistic miracle

stops.name: Bologna, Santa Maria della Pugliola: the first school
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia dates the foundation of the studium to 1223; the convent no longer stands and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: Francis of Assisi, who distrusts books in the hands of men sworn to poverty, sends Anthony a short letter of permission and thereby opens the first Franciscan school of theology, in a convent in the Pugliole quarter of the city of lawyers. The friars who will argue the order's case for the next century are trained here. Francis attaches one condition, and the letter carrying it runs to three sentences: that the spirit of prayer and devotion not be put out by the study.
stops.quote: To Brother Anthony, my bishop, Brother Francis sends his greetings. It is my pleasure that thou teach theology to the brethren, provided, however, that as the Rule prescribes, the spirit of prayer and devotion may not be extinguished. Farewell.
stops.quote_source: Letter of Francis of Assisi to Anthony, c. 1224, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The site of the convent of Santa Maria della Pugliola, Bologna, first Franciscan studium

stops.name: Bologna, the psalter taken and brought back
stops.date_confidence: legend; placed before 1231 and otherwise undated
stops.campa: A novice leaves the order in the night and takes with him the psalter Anthony teaches from, the one with his own notes in the margins, which is the working tool of the school and cannot be replaced. Anthony prays for its return rather than sending after the man. The novice comes back, restores the book, and asks to be readmitted. This is where the tradition puts the origin of his patronage of lost things, and the tradition is all there is: no contemporary source carries the story at all.
suggested_refs: The psalter reported preserved at the Franciscan friary of Bologna

stops.name: Montpellier, the lector sent north of the sea
stops.date_confidence: the teaching at Montpellier is reported by both encyclopedias as tradition rather than from a document
stops.campa: The order sends its first lector into the Midi, where a war of religion has been running for fifteen years and the Church is losing the argument in the towns. He teaches the friars at Montpellier, a university city with a medical faculty and a heretic problem. A story told about this house has him kneeling in choir at the hour he was also seen preaching elsewhere in the town, in two places at once. The encyclopedias that repeat it name no witness and cite no document.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan house at Montpellier and the medieval university

stops.name: Le Puy-en-Velay, guardian of the house
stops.date_confidence: New Advent gives 1224 for the guardianship; the research pool's geography lens gave 1225, and the two are not reconciled
stops.campa: He is made guardian of the friary at Le Puy, under the volcanic rock with the cathedral built up its side, on one of the great roads to Compostela. A guardian is a local superior: he keeps the house, the alms, the discipline, and the peace among a dozen men. It is the first office of any kind he has held, four years after being nobody at the Chapter of Mats. He holds it briefly. Within a year he is on the road again, and the next four places the record puts him in are Arles, Toulouse, Bourges, and Limoges.
stops.quote: Just as a tower defends a fortress, so humility of heart defends bodily chastity from the darts of fornication.
stops.quote_source: Sermon for the Second Sunday of Lent, Sermones Dominicales et Festivi, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Franciscan convent at Le Puy-en-Velay, on the Via Podiensis

stops.name: Arles, the provincial chapter of Provence
stops.date_confidence: the year is disputed: standard Franciscan chronology gives 1224 or 1225, English Wikipedia gives 1226; the chapter is provincial, not general
stops.campa: The friars of Provence assemble at Arles and Anthony preaches on the title nailed to the cross. Brother Monaldo, looking up at the doorway, sees Francis of Assisi standing there with his arms raised over the room, blessing it. Francis is in Italy and has not left it, and will be dead within two years. The brothers in the hall are the only witnesses, and the account of what they saw is written down decades afterwards by a man who was an infant at the time.
suggested_refs: Bonaventure, Legenda Maior, for the vision reported of Brother Monaldo at Arles

stops.name: Toulouse, preaching in the Cathar capital
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1225 by Italian Wikipedia; the tradition that he taught in the university is later and the university itself is founded in 1229
stops.campa: Toulouse is the city the Albigensian war was fought for, changing hands twice, its count excommunicated, its walls rebuilt by women carrying stones. Into this Anthony brings the only weapon his order allows him, which is argument: scripture set against scripture in the open, in the language of the street, against men who know their own texts perfectly well. Simon de Montfort's army had been through the same streets with the other method. Whether anyone in Toulouse could hear a friar preach over the memory of that is not a question the sources ask.
suggested_refs: The Albigensian Crusade and the Franciscan preaching mission in Languedoc

stops.name: Bourges, preaching to the synod
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1225 by Italian Wikipedia; no day
stops.campa: The Primate of Aquitaine calls a synod at Bourges, and the friar is asked to preach to it: archbishop, bishops, abbots, canons, the whole apparatus of the French Church seated in front of him in the new cathedral. Four years earlier he was washing pots at a hermitage in Romagna. He addresses Simon de Sully to his face on the conduct of his office, in the room, with the man's suffragans listening. Not a word of what he said is recorded. The synod sits in November 1225.
suggested_refs: The synod of Bourges of November 1225 under Archbishop Simon de Sully

stops.name: Limoges, custos of the Limousin
stops.date_confidence: New Advent gives 1226 for the custody; the grotto retreat is local tradition without documentary support
stops.campa: He is made custos of the Limousin, responsible for the friaries of a whole region, and spends the year on the roads between them. Local memory in half a dozen villages keeps a cave, a rock, a spring where he is supposed to have prayed alone, and one grotto outside Limoges has a chapel built over it that pilgrims still walk to. The documents give him an administrative title and nothing more. The caves and the springs are local memory only, and no charter or chronicle stands behind any of them.
suggested_refs: The grotto chapel outside Limoges associated with his retreats

stops.name: The Porziuncola, made provincial minister at thirty-two
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia gives the Pentecost chapter of 30 May 1227; English Wikipedia's bare 1226 contradicts it and is not followed
stops.campa: Francis has been dead eight months. The chapter that meets at Pentecost elects a new minister general and parcels out the provinces, and Anthony is given northern Italy: Lombardy, the Veneto, Friuli, Istria, the whole arc from Milan to the Adriatic. He is thirty-two years old and six years a friar, and he has never governed anything larger than a single friary in the Auvergne. In the same fields, in 1221, no minister would take him at all. The appointment is dated 30 May 1227.
suggested_refs: The Pentecost general chapter of 1227 at the Porziuncola

stops.name: Trieste, the province at its eastern edge
stops.date_confidence: placed within the provincialate of 1227-1230; the sources give a list of houses rather than dated visits
stops.campa: The jurisdiction runs out to the head of the Adriatic, where Italian gives way to Slovene and the Patriarch of Aquileia rules a march rather than a diocese. Anthony travels it on foot with a companion, as the Rule requires, checking houses, settling disputes among friars, licensing new foundations. He is a middle-aged administrator walking a long circuit, and the walking is most of the job. Nothing miraculous is recorded of these years on the eastern coast.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan houses of the Adriatic march under the Patriarchate of Aquileia

stops.name: Pola, a convent founded in Istria
stops.date_confidence: attributed to the provincialate of 1227-1230 without a precise year
stops.campa: A Franciscan house is founded at Pola in his time as provincial, inside a town still holding a Roman amphitheatre entire and a temple to Augustus in daily use as a church. The order is a year or two past the death of its founder and expanding faster than it can train men to fill the houses it is being given. Anthony signs the foundations and moves on down the coast. Istria and Dalmatia will keep Franciscans continuously from these years to the present day.
suggested_refs: The medieval Franciscan foundation at Pula, Istria

stops.name: Gemona del Friuli, the northern limit
stops.date_confidence: listed among the Friulian visitation places without a dated visit
stops.campa: The visitation reaches Gemona, under the wall of the Julian Alps, where the road down from Germany comes out into the plain and every merchant, soldier, and pilgrim crossing the mountains has to pass under the town. It is the top of his province, and the friars here are hosts to the whole traffic of the pass. From Gemona the circuit turns south again, down the Tagliamento, through Treviso and Venice and then to Padua, where a convent has been founded in his time as provincial.
suggested_refs: The Alpine road through Gemona and the Friulian Franciscan houses

stops.name: Venice, the province among the merchants
stops.date_confidence: listed among the provincial visits; no dated occasion survives
stops.campa: The richest city on the sea falls inside his province, twenty-five years after its fleet sacked Constantinople and came home with the bronze horses. Anthony preaches to merchants for most of his working life, in Padua and Rimini and Bologna as here, and the sermon he returns to is always the same: on what possession does to the man who holds it. The city listens, gives generously to the friars, and goes on lending at interest the next morning. Whether he expected anything else, the sermons do not say.
stops.quote: Solicitude for material things rends the soul; thus distracted, it divides it. The devil seizes the divided soul and thereby kills it.
stops.quote_source: Sermon for the Fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, Sermones Dominicales et Festivi, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The early Franciscan presence in Venice before the building of the Frari

stops.name: Ferrara, the newborn who spoke
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated, placed by tradition within the provincial years
stops.campa: A nobleman of Ferrara looks at his newborn son, decides the child cannot be his, and accuses his wife publicly, which in that century is close to a sentence. The woman brings the baby to Anthony in front of the household. He asks the infant who its father is, and the infant, a few days old, turns its head and names the man standing there. The marriage holds. The tellings do not give the woman's name, or the child's, or say what became of either of them.
suggested_refs: The Ferrara legend of the speaking infant in later Franciscan legendary

stops.name: Rome, the Lent preached before Gregory IX
stops.date_confidence: attested to Lent 1228 by Italian Wikipedia; the pope's exact words are given in three different wordings by three sources
stops.campa: Called to the papal court, he preaches the Lenten meditations before Gregory IX and the cardinals, and does it from memory, moving through the whole of scripture without a book in front of him. The court is composed of professional readers and it is impressed. The pope gives him a title that sticks to him: the Ark of the Testament, the chest the Law was kept in. A cardinal commissions from him a set of sermons for the feasts, and he begins writing them down.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Pope Gregory IX at Rome; the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) gives 'Ark of the Covenant', English Wikipedia 'jewel case of the Bible', Italian Wikipedia the title 'Doctor Arca testamenti'
suggested_refs: The Sermones in Festivitates, commissioned in this period

stops.name: Assisi, the body of Francis carried into the new basilica
stops.date_confidence: the translation is attested to Pentecost, 25 May 1230; Italian Wikipedia's 25 June is the inauguration date and does not match
stops.campa: At Pentecost the bones of Francis of Assisi are carried in procession into the Lower Church of the basilica raised over them, and buried under the rock in secret by the commune's decision, so that no other city can steal them. Anthony walks in that procession, four years a minister of the order Francis left behind. He is one of the small number of men still alive who stood in the field at the Chapter of Mats nine years earlier and watched the man himself divide up the world among them.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di San Francesco d'Assisi and the concealed burial of 25 May 1230

stops.name: The Porziuncola, the office laid down
stops.date_confidence: attested by New Advent to the general chapter of 30 May 1230
stops.campa: Five days after the burial the general chapter sits in the same fields where he was nobody in 1221, and Anthony asks to be released from the province. Three years of visitations, foundations, and disputes have used him up, and he tells them he wants to preach and to write and nothing else. They let him go, and elect another man to Lombardy and the Veneto. He is thirty-five. He wants a room in Padua and the season of Lent, and that is what he is given.
suggested_refs: The general chapter of Assisi, 30 May 1230

stops.name: Rome, the embassy over the Testament of Francis
stops.date_confidence: the bull Quo elongati is dated 28 September 1230; the delegation's arrival in Rome is not dated
stops.campa: The order is splitting over what its founder actually bound it to, and specifically over whether the Testament Francis dictated on his deathbed has the force of law. A delegation goes to Rome to ask, and Anthony is on it, four months after laying down his province. The delegation's arrival is not dated in any source. Gregory IX answers with the bull Quo elongati, dated 28 September 1230: the Testament does not bind, and the friars may use goods held for them by others.
suggested_refs: The bull Quo elongati, 28 September 1230

stops.name: La Verna, months on the mountain
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia gives a stay of several months in 1230; no month is specified
stops.campa: He goes up to the beech forest and the split rock in the Casentino, the mountain Count Orlando di Chiusi gave Francis in 1213 and where Francis received the stigmata six years before he died. Anthony stays some months, through an autumn on a mountain that is snowed on early. There is no record of anything he did up there. It is the last stretch of his life in which he is neither preaching nor dying. He comes down before the winter, into the Lent of 1231.
suggested_refs: The Santuario della Verna, given by Count Orlando di Chiusi at San Leo, 8 May 1213

stops.name: Padua, Santa Maria Mater Domini: the last Lent
stops.date_confidence: the Lenten cycle of 1231 is attested; the crowd figures of 30,000 come from hagiography
stops.campa: He preaches every day of Lent in a university town of maybe fifteen thousand people, and the accounts say thirty thousand come, from the countryside, sleeping in the fields to hold their place. The shops shut. What he preaches on, here as everywhere, is usury and restitution and the settling of quarrels, in a city where the money trade is the business of the university's own lawyers. He is already ill when the season starts, and he preaches through it anyway.
stops.quote: Where thy treasure is, there also is thy heart.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Anthony preaching at a usurer's funeral, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The church of Santa Maria Mater Domini, later absorbed into the basilica as the Cappella della Madonna Mora

stops.name: Verona, before Ezzelino da Romano
stops.date_confidence: Italian Wikipedia dates the Verona embassy to May 1231
stops.campa: Ezzelino da Romano holds the March of Treviso by terror and has Count Rizzardo di San Bonifacio's people in his prisons. Anthony, worn out and two months from death, travels to Verona to ask for their release. He is received, he is heard out, and he gets nothing. The embassy is dated to May 1231, and what was said in the room is not recorded. Ezzelino holds the March by the same methods for another twenty-eight years, and the prisoners stay where they are.
suggested_refs: Ezzelino III da Romano and the prisoners of the March of Treviso

stops.name: Camposampiero, the cell in the walnut tree
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1231; the walnut-tree cell and the vision of the Christ child are traditional
stops.campa: Count Tiso gives him the use of a wood on his land north of Padua, and the friars build him a platform in the branches of a great walnut tree where he can sleep off the ground and be left alone to finish his sermons. The tradition adds that Tiso, passing at night, saw light in the cell and looked in, and saw Anthony holding a child. No one else reports it. The illness that had been on him all spring gets worse in this wood, and he does not walk out of it.
suggested_refs: The Santuario del Noce at Camposampiero, on the site of the walnut tree
The competing diagnoses of his final illness: dropsy in the older accounts, ergotism in the modern ones

stops.name: Arcella, the cart stops short of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 June 1231; the New Advent text as fetched names Vercelli instead of Arcella, and gives his age as 36 against Wikipedia's 35
stops.campa: They put him on an ox-cart to carry him back to his own convent in Padua and he does not last the road. At Arcella, on the northern edge of the city, they turn in at the Poor Clares' house and carry him inside. He makes his confession, is anointed, and sings a hymn to the Virgin. The friars in the room record that he lifted his eyes and stayed looking at something for a long while before he spoke. He is thirty-five, or thirty-six, and eleven years a Franciscan.
stops.quote_source: His last words by tradition, on seeing the Host: I see my Lord (Italian Wikipedia, 'Antonio di Padova')
suggested_refs: The Santuario dell'Arcella, built on the site of the Poor Clare hospice

stops.name: Padua, the burial four days on
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 June 1231 by Italian Wikipedia
stops.campa: It takes four days and an armed escort to bring him the two miles from Arcella into the city, through a crowd that has to be held off the coffin the whole way. He is buried the same evening at Santa Maria Mater Domini, the small church he had asked for, beside the convent he had founded two years before. The reports of cures at the grave begin at once and do not stop. Inside a year the dossier of them will be carried to a pope. They are still writing entries into it while the ground over him is fresh.
suggested_refs: The dossier of miracles at the tomb, compiled at Padua for the canonization process

stops.name: Spoleto, canonized in under a year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 May 1232 by both encyclopedias
stops.campa: Three hundred and fifty-two days after the death at Arcella, Gregory IX declares him a saint at Spoleto, on the evidence of a dossier of miracles assembled in Padua at speed. It is among the fastest canonizations the Church has ever performed and the pope, who had heard him preach in Rome four years before, does not appear to have needed much convincing. The city that had to be held off the coffin is given a feast day for its friar: the thirteenth of June.
suggested_refs: The canonization bull of Gregory IX, Spoleto, 30 May 1232

stops.name: Padua, the basilica goes up around the grave
stops.date_confidence: construction begins c. 1232 and the building is substantially complete by 1301-1310
stops.campa: Building starts within about a year of the canonization and does not stop for seventy years: domes on the Byzantine pattern, brick, minarets that are not minarets, the small burial church swallowed whole and kept inside as a chapel. Paduans do not call it by his name. They call it Il Santo, the way you refer to someone you assume everyone in the room already knows. A responsory written for the new feast, Si quaeris miracula, is the piece of Latin that hands him the office of finding what is lost. Only a fragment of it can now be verified.
stops.quote_source: Friar Julian of Speyer, responsory 'Si quaeris miracula' (13th century), fragment as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913); the complete text could not be verified from a fetched source
suggested_refs: Titian's three fresco scenes of Anthony's miracles for the Scuola del Santo, Padua, 1511
The fourteenth-century fresco cycles of the basilica complex, UNESCO listed 2021
sources: Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Saint Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Padua, the tomb opened before Bonaventure
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 April 1263; English Wikipedia's 'thirty years after his death' is a round figure for this same event and not a separate opening
stops.campa: Thirty-two years in the ground, and the remains are lifted for translation into the finished basilica. The minister general of the order, Bonaventure, is there when the coffin is opened. The body has gone to dust. The tongue has not: it comes out of the dust whole, red, and soft, and Bonaventure takes it in his hands in front of everyone and speaks to it. It is set aside as a relic. Everyone who reports what was in the coffin that day belongs to the cult, and nobody examines it.
stops.quote: O Blessed Tongue that always praised the Lord, and made others bless Him, now it is evident what great merit thou hast before God.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure at the opening of the tomb, 1263, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Cappella del Tesoro of the basilica, begun 1691, housing the reliquaries of the chin and tongue

stops.name: Vatican City, the title Doctor Evangelicus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 January 1946
stops.campa: Seven hundred and fifteen years after Arcella, Pius XII adds him to the doctors of the Church and gives him the title Doctor Evangelicus, for the freshness of the Gospel in his writing. The decision rests on the sermon collections, the Sunday cycle and the feast-day cycle, the books he was still working on in the walnut tree at Camposampiero when he ran out of time. The letter is dated 16 January 1946 and is called Exulta Lusitania felix, rejoice, happy Portugal.
suggested_refs: The apostolic letter Exulta Lusitania felix, 16 January 1946

stops.name: Padua, the tomb opened again with instruments
stops.date_confidence: authorized by John Paul II in January 1981; the afterlife record gives 6 January for the opening
stops.campa: John Paul II authorizes an examination and a team of anatomists and pathologists opens the tomb, the first formal reopening of the modern era. The bones are photographed, measured, and put back, and the vocal apparatus recovered in the course of it is enshrined separately from that year, so that the larynx joins the chin and the tongue in the treasury. Outside, in the piazza, people go on writing notes about lost husbands and lost papers and leaving them at the marble.
suggested_refs: The 1981 scientific recognition of the relics and the enshrinement of the vocal apparatus
